subject: biology
title: Recombinant DNA technology
key_idea: Recombinant DNA combines DNA from different organisms. A gene is obtained, cut into a vector such as a plasmid and put into a host cell. If the gene is expressed, the host makes a useful protein, such as human insulin.

blocks.text: Genetic engineering is the deliberate manipulation of genetic material to modify the characteristics of an organism. A gene is transferred so that it is expressed in the new organism.

items.meaning: DNA made by joining DNA from two or more different organisms.
An organism that contains a gene from another species.
A carrier, such as a plasmid, used to take a gene into a host cell.

blocks.text: The genetic code is universal, and so are transcription and translation. A gene from one species can therefore be read in another.

items: **From the donor's DNA**: restriction endonucleases cut the DNA either side of the gene. They cut at specific base sequences, often leaving short single-stranded 'sticky ends'.
**From mRNA**: the donor cell makes lots of mRNA for the protein. Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA (cDNA) from it, and DNA polymerase makes the second strand. The cDNA has no introns.
**Chemically**: a 'gene machine' joins nucleotides in the right order, using the known amino acid sequence.
A gene can be cut out with restriction enzymes, made from mRNA with reverse transcriptase, or built in a gene machine.
The universal genetic code allows a gene to work in another species.

sections.heading: Inserting the gene into a host

blocks.text: The gene is joined into a vector with the right control sequences, then the vector is taken up by host cells.

diagram.alt: The steps in making a recombinant plasmid and a transformed host.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps of genetic engineering with a plasmid in order.
steps: Obtain the gene and add a promoter and terminator
Cut the plasmid with the same restriction enzyme, to give matching sticky ends
Mix the gene and plasmid. Sticky ends base-pair and DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbones
Transform host cells with the recombinant plasmid
Identify transformed cells using a marker gene
Culture the transformed cells so they express the gene

items: **Restriction endonucleases** cut the plasmid at the same sequence, so the cut ends are complementary to the gene's ends.
**DNA ligase** forms phosphodiester bonds to seal the gene into the plasmid, making recombinant DNA.
A **promoter** must be added to the gene, because the host's RNA polymerase needs it to start transcription. A terminator marks the end.
Host cells take up the plasmid when they are treated to make them permeable, for example with calcium ions and heat shock, or by electroporation, which uses an electric pulse.
Only a few cells take up the plasmid, so they have to be identified.
Restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins, and the promoter lets the gene be expressed.
Host cells must be made to take up the recombinant plasmid.

blocks.text: Marker genes show which cells have taken up the gene and are expressing it.

items: The marker gene is placed in the vector next to the desired gene.
A gene for a **fluorescent product**, such as green fluorescent protein (GFP), makes transformed cells glow under UV light. This confirms the gene is expressed.
Antibiotic-resistance genes can also be used: only cells with the plasmid survive on a medium containing the antibiotic.
**Gene editing** is a form of genetic engineering. It inserts, deletes or replaces DNA at specific sites in the genome.
A marker gene shows which cells carry the new gene.
Gene editing changes DNA at a chosen site.

blocks.text: Genetically modified organisms can produce human proteins for use as drugs. Microorganisms, animals and plants are all used.

items: **Insulin** for diabetes is made by bacteria or yeast carrying the human gene.
**Factor VIII** is a blood-clotting protein, used to treat haemophilia.
**Adenosine deaminase** is used to treat a form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
Recombinant proteins are identical to human ones, so there is less chance of an immune reaction than with proteins from animals.
They can be made in large amounts, and are free from infectious agents that could be in donated human blood or tissue.
Production can be scaled up in fermenters, and it avoids the ethical objections to using animals.
GM organisms make human proteins such as insulin and factor VIII.
Recombinant proteins are safe, pure and made in quantity.

checks.q: Explain the roles of restriction endonuclease and DNA ligase in making recombinant DNA.
checks.a: Restriction endonuclease cuts the plasmid and the gene at specific base sequences, leaving matching sticky ends. DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbones of the gene and plasmid to seal them together.

checks.q: Explain why a promoter must be transferred with the gene into a bacterium.
checks.a: RNA polymerase in the host must bind to the promoter to start transcription. Without the promoter the gene would not be transcribed, so the protein would not be made.

checks.q: Explain how a gene for a fluorescent protein can be used to show that a gene has been expressed.
checks.a: The fluorescent marker gene is transferred with the desired gene. Cells that express the transferred genes make the fluorescent protein, so they glow under UV light and can be identified.

items: **In vitro**: the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) copies fragments in a machine.
**In vivo**: transformed host cells are cultured, and copy the fragment each time the cells divide.
Promoter and terminator regions are added to the fragment so that it is expressed in the host.
You must be able to interpret information on recombinant DNA technology.
Evaluate ethical, financial and social issues of its use and ownership in agriculture, industry and medicine.
Balance the humanitarian benefits (for example food or medicine for poor countries) against opposition from environmentalists and anti-globalisation activists.
Relate recombinant DNA technology to gene therapy, where a working allele is delivered to a patient's cells.
You do not need to recall specific marker genes in a written paper.
Drugs can be produced using GM **microorganisms** (for example bacteria making insulin), **animals** and **plants**.
Animals and plants can be modified to secrete the drug in milk, eggs or plant tissue, from which it is purified.
Microorganisms grow quickly and cheaply in fermenters, and make large amounts of the product.
Learn the exact definition: **recombinant DNA** is DNA formed by combining DNA from different sources.
Genes can be extracted from a donor, synthesised from the donor's mRNA, or synthesised chemically from nucleotides.
DNA polymerase makes the second strand of cDNA, and reverse transcriptase makes the first.

The advantages of recombinant human proteins (insulin, factor VIII, adenosine deaminase) are: exact human structure, fewer side effects, no risk of infection, ethical acceptability and large-scale production.
Describe the principles of genetic engineering: isolating a gene from one organism and placing it in another using a suitable vector.
The techniques include restriction enzymes, plasmids and DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA with the desired gene.
**Electroporation** uses a short electric pulse to make the cell membrane permeable so that the plasmid can enter.
